nameStory: This aquatic buttercup gets its name from its incredibly fine, thread-like underwater leaves that look almost like green hair floating in the water. The 'water-crowfoot' part refers to the shape of its segmented leaves, which early botanists thought resembled a crow's foot. It's a fitting name for a plant that spends most of its life submerged, with leaves so delicate they feel like silk threads when you run them through your fingers.
description: Thread-leaved water-crowfoot is a small aquatic plant that lives almost entirely underwater in slow-moving streams, ponds, and lakes. It produces delicate white flowers with bright yellow centers that float on the water surface, looking like tiny daisies scattered across the water. The plant has two types of leaves - the underwater ones are finely divided into thread-like segments, while any leaves near the surface may be more rounded. This is one of New England's rarest buttercups, with very few confirmed sightings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Underwater leaves are finely divided into thread-like segments that feel soft and silky when touched, creating a feathery appearance that sways gracefully with water movement

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with exactly five petals and bright yellow centers that float on or just above the water surface, resembling miniature daisies

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows completely submerged in slow-moving or still water, with only the flowers reaching the surface during blooming period

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops rounded seed heads that mature into bristly fruits, feeling rough and spiky to the touch when ripe

habitat: Found in slow-flowing streams, quiet ponds, and shallow lake margins with clean, cool water. Prefers areas with gentle currents or still water where its delicate thread-like leaves won't be damaged by strong flow. Most likely to be found in northern New England's pristine mountain ponds and beaver meadows.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water temperatures warm, with thread-like leaves becoming visible underwater in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period when small white flowers appear floating on the water surface, making the plant most visible and identifiable.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and bristly seed heads develop, while underwater foliage may begin to die back as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely in frozen waters, surviving as seeds or rootstock depending on whether it's growing as an annual or perennial.

funFact: This remarkable plant can actually photosynthesize underwater using its thread-like leaves, making it one of the few flowering plants that can live its entire life cycle submerged except for the brief moment when it sends up flowers to reproduce!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with yellow water-crowfoot, which has similar thread-like underwater leaves but produces yellow flowers instead of white ones. Remember: white flowers with exactly five petals means thread-leaved, while yellow flowers often indicate its cousin species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'crowfoot,' this plant is actually a true buttercup in the Ranunculus genus. The term 'crowfoot' is an old name used for many buttercup species, referring to the divided leaf shape that resembles a bird's foot, though in this aquatic species the 'foot' has been refined into delicate underwater threads.
compareHints: Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage. It differs from yellow water-crowfoot by having exactly five petals instead of more, and from other aquatic buttercups by its preference for slower waters and shorter, more finely divided leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
